codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot isolate the reward’s effect as specified because the planned three-week overlap is only one week and the checklist prompt changes on a wave-specific schedule.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design rests on a fixed 10-jobs-per-week audit sample and two waves, with no sample-size check showing that a 5-point difference in audited compliance could actually be detected. The 'inconclusive' outcome is therefore likely, and the reward's incremental value over the workflow fixes is never cleanly separated, because the prefilled-default change is introduced in both waves during the reward period.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, no penalties, verifiable records, audit guardrails and a default-based exit make it approvable, but a 30-minute team break is a modest reward and the 15-point private target plus the verification burden could blunt salience and durability.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot is not launchable until it defines a payout quality gate, because safety compliance on uncredited jobs can fall without triggering either pause rule.

claude.worst_flaw: Weeks 3–4 give only about half the crews to compare, with no sample-size or power estimate, and the 5-point thresholds have no uncertainty rule. Meanwhile, appeals and corrections rely on one programme owner, with no replayable event or policy versions and no staffed SLA.

holistic.reason: Union-friendly, verification-based, and well-guarded against gaming and unsafe shortcuts, but a one-off 30-minute team release-time reward is modest and unlikely to be noticed strongly or sustain the habit after it ends.

claude.worst_flaw: Operability rests on existing support channels without replayable event or policy versioning or independent shadow validation of the credit rule, and the crew-level lottery with roughly 300 technicians gives a 5-point decision threshold little power, with no pre-specified sample size or uncertainty handling.

codex.worst_flaw: When the app is unavailable, jobs completed safely using the approved paper fallback still lower the crew’s digital completion rate, creating peer pressure to avoid the fallback.

holistic.reason: Union-co-designed, independently verified, gaming-resistant with stop rules and a staggered rollout, but a meal reward is modest, tracking via crew averages may be diluted, and durability beyond the reward depends on the app fixes and defaults sticking.

claude.worst_flaw: Groups earn credit only for reviews that go back to the assigned reviewer within eight staffed hours. Nothing caps how much review work lands on the rotating primary, and nothing tracks author-side delays, so crediting by group could hide overload or knock-on delays on other work. Operability is also thin: there is no replayable event history or versioned policy, the appeals process has no staff beyond the pilot owner, and the rules are never shadow-tested on real past PRs before launch.

codex.worst_flaw: The decision to repeat the reward hinges on a two-week comparison of just two groups, where a 10-point gap could reflect differences in PR complexity or reviewer availability.

holistic.reason: The proposal fixes the real bottleneck (a rota, protected review time and queue order) and has careful audit and anti-gaming safeguards. But the credit rules are intricate, the reward is only one paid hour per group, and the engineers who are sceptical may find the tracking heavy, so I would approve it with some doubt about how many people notice it and keep trying.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward decision relies on a two-week comparison between two groups without checking whether differences in PR complexity or reviewers working across groups could explain the result.

claude.worst_flaw: Rewards rely on group-level on-time rates checked by a lead's six-case weekly sample, but there is no replayable event log, staffed appeal process, or independent shadow validation. The design also leaves unresolved how the rotation concentrates credit on duty reviewers while each person's private share is measured against 'assigned' reviews.

holistic.reason: Fixing the queue first, an objective PR-record metric, private individual feedback, a quality-sampling pause rule and a staggered comparison make this credible to sceptical engineers, but the rules are detailed, the reward is only one paid hour, and the 45-minute weekly sampling load and two-group comparison are thin, so excitement and durability are moderate.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design compares only two review groups, so the reward effect cannot be separated from group differences, and no outcome, cost or harm thresholds apply to the comparison itself. Quality is tracked only through a weekly five-PR sample, with no formal appeals, versioned event history or post-payout quality measure.

codex.worst_flaw: Approvals can earn credit by satisfying merge rules alone, while specific change requests require author follow-through, so reviewers can improve the measured on-time rate by approving more readily.

holistic.reason: It fixes the real bottleneck (queue, rotation, protected time) before any reward, uses a team-level reward with no rankings, and has a quality check and a clear decision rule, but the credit rules are complicated and the reward is small, so engagement from sceptical engineers is uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot can meet every success criterion even if nurses rarely use the kiosk, because it measures observed hand-hygiene compliance and tracks kiosk entries only as a raw count.

claude.worst_flaw: Ward results rest on monthly observer audits that may have small, uneven numbers of observed opportunities, and the design has no minimum sample, no confidence handling and no appeal process, so a meal decision or pause can hinge on noise from a handful of observations.

holistic.reason: Well-designed audit-based reward with safeguards, staggered controls, and a fix-the-workflow focus, but a team meal for hand hygiene is a weak, delayed incentive that nurses may barely notice, and gains may fade once it ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The programme could reward wards and recommend repeating the incentive without ever measuring whether nurses log eligible hand-hygiene moments in the kiosk.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never says what the kiosk logs are for or how good they are: entries earn nothing and are only spot-checked for eligibility, so the scenario's main asset could fill up with incomplete, unvalidated data while the reward rests on a handful of monthly observer audits that are open to observer effects.

holistic.reason: The design rewards audited behaviour rather than kiosk logging, fixes workflow first, includes a staggered rollout, safeguards and a clear stop rule, but a once-per-two-months team meal is a weak, delayed motivator that nurses may barely notice, and with three wards the lift may fade once it ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The design rewards ward-level observed audit compliance but never reconciles this with the scenario's stated goal of getting nurses to log moments in the kiosk. As a result, kiosk adoption has no target or measure of success. Hawthorne-biased, sparse monthly audits are also left as the only outcome, with no independent shadow validation or staffed appeal path.

codex.worst_flaw: The design uses observed hand-hygiene compliance as its sole success metric, leaving the hospital unable to tell whether nurses reliably log eligible moments in the kiosk.

holistic.reason: Rewarding audited outcomes rather than kiosk entries, fixing the workflow first, and using a staggered design with clear stop rules is well controlled, but a single team meal is a weak, delayed motivator and the baked-in kiosk and board fixes are the only likely sources of lasting change.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward decision hinges on a two-percentage-point difference, but the design gives no rule for deciding whether the three-week comparison across teams can distinguish that effect from noise.

claude.worst_flaw: Ten tickets sampled per week across 60 agents is too few to catch irrelevant-link gaming reliably, and the appeal process has no staff or timeline, so wrong reversals have no dependable fix.

holistic.reason: The design is careful, with a verifiable counting rule, a staggered pilot, guardrails and no punishment for missed weeks. But the reward is small (paid learning time at team level), the rule is complicated to explain, and the QA sampling and credit reversals add friction, so it may not be noticed or sustain behaviour change once the reward stops.

codex.worst_flaw: The rollout decision relies on a two-week comparison with no predefined minimum sample, uncertainty rule, or adjustment for changes in ticket mix.

claude.worst_flaw: The decision metric (2 repeat contacts per 100) has no stated baseline or check that it can be detected at about 60 agents and paired teams over two weeks, and the existing CSAT bonus could push agents to rush or game articles, yet the design never reconciles the two.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with verified credit, QA sampling, staggered rollout and a repeat-contact outcome metric, but the 15-point target, one hour of time off and heavy verification complexity may feel modest or burdensome, and a four-week reward may not sustain habits once it ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The planned comparison uses the three weeks when both groups are earning rewards, so it cannot isolate the incentive’s effect over plain feedback.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no individual appeal process and no replayable event and policy history: one admin fixes counting errors and the QA lead alone decides when paused rewards resume, with no independent shadow validation and no staffed dispute path for agents.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with verification, staggered rollout, QA sampling and a CSAT guardrail, but the rules are complex to explain, the team-level reward is small and diffuse, and it adds QA and eligibility overhead that may fade once the prizes end.
